subtype_info: central nervous system tuberculosis with sellar-suprasellar tuberculoma and meningitis
title: Pediatric sellar-suprasellar tuberculosis: A case report and review of the literature
case_text:
A 17-year-old male without a medical history presented progressive symptoms during the past month, consisting of headaches, decreased visual acuity, and visual field impairment with right temporal hemianopia. The clinical examination found a conscious patient, slightly feverish, pulse was 78/min, and his blood pressure was 120/76 mm Hg. The lung examination was clear on auscultation. The chest radiograph was normal. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain shows a sellar-suprasellar lesion, isointense to hypointense on T1, isointense to hyperintense on T2 [Figure 1], enhanced heterogeneously with gadolinium [Figures 2a and b], with other small lesions in the posterior cerebral fossa and the hypothalamus. On investigation, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) fluid analysis revealed lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, and a high protein level. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for M. tuberculosis was positive in the CSF, and the results of the Interferon-Gamma Release Assays and Mantoux test were positive. Evaluation of pituitary function, on the other hand, revealed normal hormonal levels. All other serological tests, including the HIV test, yielded negative results.
Based on clinical features, neuroimaging, and investigations, a diagnosis of meningitis tuberculosis with cerebral and pituitary tuberculoma was made. Treatment for tuberculosis was initiated with a 2-month combination of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 7 months of isoniazid and rifampicin, associated with corticosteroid therapy, and the evolution was marked by the clinical improvement of the patient, even on the radiological level, by the disappearance of the lesion [Figures 2c and d].

Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Tuberculosis
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: central nervous system tuberculosis with sellar-suprasellar tuberculoma and meningitis
